3.text: Then begins his trial, which lasts one summer, sometimes two or even three

4.text: summers. All this time the suitor leads a very hard life. He rises first in

5.text: the morning, and retires last at night. Often he is not even given a place

6.text: in the sleeping-room, but stays in the outer tent or in the open air. Most

7.text: of his time is spent with the herd. He carries burdens, hauls heavily-loaded

8.text: sledges, mends and repairs broken utensils. He has to please the girl’s father,

9.text: her elder brothers, and other male members of the family. If one of the old

10.text: people reproaches him and calls him names, he has to bear it patiently, and

11.text: is even expected to agree. When the old people are ill-tempered, — as many

12.text: Chukchee are, — they may decline food and shelter to the poor suitor. Then

13.text: he has to endure the pangs of hunger and cold while performing his work.

14.text: If the girl likes him, she will try to give him some meat; or he may steal

15.text: some food and devour it in haste, lest somebody should see it and report

16.text: him to the father. Even then, after two or three months of continual toil,

17.text: he may be driven away without any apparent reason. “This is no cause of

18.text: resentment,” I was told by the Chukchee; “but only a weakling consents to

19.text: go. A good strong man remains and works on without food, without place

20.text: in the sleeping-room, and even without hope.” To desist, and return home
20.note: Closing curly quote (U+201D); machine draft carried a literal backslash-quote sequence. §1/§5.6 — quotes are always curly, never keyed straight.

21.text: without a bride, is considered a humiliation for a young man. His father

22.text: will say, “So you are really bad. If you were good, you would not be sent

23.note: Closing curly quote (U+201D); machine draft carried a literal backslash-quote sequence. §1/§5.6.

24.text: After the first few months the father of the bride usually somewhat relents,

25.text: and the conditions of life of thé suitor become less severe. From that time

26.text: on, it is not thought becoming to send him away without serious reason.

27.text: The suitor also begins to insist on his matrimonial rights. Often he acquires

28.text: them after several months of struggle. Of course, this depends largely upon

29.text: the woman herself. Some fathers, however, keep guard over their daughters.

30.text: For instance, in the night-time, after the suitor is admitted to sleep in the

31.text: inner room, the father bids the girl lie down in the corner, and takes his

32.text: place by her side, so that she is inaccessible to the suitor. I was also told

33.text: of cases where the suitor, in his passion, tries to take the bride by force from
33.note: A short diagonal stray mark sits between 'bride' and 'by' at 4x, too high and too short to be a hyphen (no horizontal stroke at mid-x-height); read as an ink speck, not type. §2.14 — a printer's blot is keyed as nothing.

34.text: the side of her father; or where he attempts to force her after all the people

35.text: are fast asleep. This, however, is not considered a serious offence.

36.text: As soon as the bridegroom becomes the actual husband, his thoughts natu-

37.text: rally turn back to his own home and herd, and he plans to take his wife home.

38.text: For this reason the girl’s father delays the marriage as long as possible, espe-

39.text: cially when he is rather short of herdsmen and the help of the bridegroom is

41.text: Lisiansky (Voyage around the World, II, p. 79) says that among the inhabitants of Kadyak the marriage-rite is

42.text: as follows: the bridegroom passes the night with the bride; in the morning he must arise very early and bring

43.text: fuel from the woods. This is considered the more important, as in many points of the island it is difficult to

44.text: get fuel because the country is quite treeless.
